summary:
SkyTrace is A 3D Temporal Explorer for NASA SPHEREx Data is an interactive web platform designed to make complex astronomical observations easier and more engaging to explore.
We developed a 3D sky explorer that lets users navigate astronomical coordinates, access real NASA SPHEREx infrared measurements, and compare images depicting the same region of space at different times. Using scientific image-processing techniques, the platform creates difference maps, estimates the significance of observed changes, and marks potential astronomical change candidates for further investigation.
SkyTrace responds to the challenge of making NASA’s extensive infrared datasets easier to visualize, understand, and explore without requiring advanced astronomical software skills. It connects raw scientific data with a more intuitive and interactive analysis experience.
The project makes space science more accessible to students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts. It also creates opportunities for education, citizen science, and later investigations into moving or variable celestial objects. Any changes identified by SkyTrace are treated as candidates for scientific validation rather than confirmed discoveries.
details:
SkyTrace: Tracing Changes Throughout the Universe

SkyTrace is an interactive web-based platform that makes NASA’s SPHEREx infrared measurements easier to access, understand, and explore. It brings together 3D sky visualization, real astronomical data, scientific image processing, and time-based analysis in one application. The main goal is to help students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts examine the universe and investigate possible changes in celestial objects over time.

The platform includes an interactive 3D celestial sphere where users can browse different regions of the sky, zoom in on areas of interest, and select locations using Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec), the coordinate system commonly used in astronomy. Once a region is selected, SkyTrace connects to its backend and retrieves available SPHEREx infrared measurements from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). These observations are provided in FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) format, which is widely used to store astronomical images and related scientific data.

SkyTrace processes the retrieved observations and allows users to compare images from the same region of the sky captured at different times. Before making a comparison, the system checks important factors such as wavelength compatibility and image quality. It then uses World Coordinate System (WCS) information to align the images, ensuring that corresponding pixels represent the same locations in the sky.

After alignment, the application calculates pixel-level differences and estimated significance values. This process creates difference maps and marks regions that may show interesting changes. These highlighted areas are treated as preliminary change candidates that need further investigation, not as confirmed astronomical discoveries.

SkyTrace takes on the challenge of making large and complex astronomy datasets easier to use. Although NASA provides a wide range of scientific data, exploring it often requires specialized software, knowledge of astronomical coordinates, and experience with scientific image processing. SkyTrace makes this simpler by combining data retrieval, visualization, and time-based analysis in one intuitive web interface. Instead of downloading and processing multiple files manually, users can browse the sky visually and examine observations through a more straightforward workflow.

The project provides several important benefits. It gives users easier access to real NASA astronomical data, supports astronomy education, and offers a convenient way to investigate regions of the sky that may have changed over time. Students can learn about infrared astronomy, celestial coordinates, scientific imaging, and the value of repeated observations. Astronomy enthusiasts can work with authentic space data, while researchers can use the platform to identify areas that may deserve more detailed study.

SkyTrace is built with TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The frontend uses React and Next.js to create a responsive and interactive web application. Three.js and React Three Fiber power the 3D celestial sphere, allowing users to move around the sky and select specific regions.

The backend uses Python and FastAPI to communicate with astronomical data services and perform scientific processing. Astropy handles FITS files, astronomical metadata, celestial coordinates, and WCS information. NumPy is used for numerical calculations and pixel-level image operations, while SciPy provides additional tools for scientific computing and image processing. The main data source is NASA/IPAC IRSA, which provides access to real SPHEREx observations. Microsoft Azure is also being considered for future cloud deployment.

What makes SkyTrace creative is the way it combines 3D sky exploration with time-based astronomical analysis. Instead of presenting observations only as files or static images, the platform lets users move through the sky, retrieve real infrared data, and compare observations from different periods. Its innovation comes from combining established astronomical methods with modern web-based visualization tools in one user-friendly environment. This makes scientific research more engaging without requiring users to handle every technical step themselves.

During development, the team focused on several key factors, including scientific reliability, data authenticity, observation compatibility, image quality, computing performance, usability, and scalability. Astronomical recordings can contain noise, instrumental artifacts, wavelength differences, and alignment errors, all of which may produce misleading changes in an image. To reduce these issues, SkyTrace uses compatibility tests, quality masking, WCS-based alignment, and difference-analysis methods.

Even with these safeguards, the change-candidate detection process still requires scientific validation. SkyTrace does not claim to confirm new astronomical discoveries. Separating the frontend visualization from the backend scientific processing also supports a clear architecture that can be improved and expanded over time.

The broader aim of SkyTrace is to reduce the distance between complex astronomical research data and general understanding. By making NASA’s infrared measurements easier to access, visualize, and compare, the project encourages scientific wonder, supports education, and opens space exploration to a wider audience. Future improvements could include support for additional space missions, more advanced analysis methods, improved tools for investigating candidates, and educational or citizen-science features.

SkyTrace shows how modern web development and scientific computing can work together to turn real NASA space data into an interactive experience. Through its combination of 3D navigation, authentic infrared observations, and time-based image comparison, the platform makes it easier for people to explore and understand a changing universe.
